newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori says jailed general to be freed.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori says jailed general to be freed.

text.p: Peru's President Alberto Fujimori said on Wednesday retired Gen. Rodolfo Robles would be freed from jail by the weekend under an amnesty that would overrule his controversial detention by the military.
"Everything is back to normal," Fujimori told reporters. "When there is one level of hierarchy, there is one head and it is the head that decides," he said.
The government-controlled Congress is expected to easily pass in Thursday's session Fujimori's rapidly-prepared bill granting an amnesty for retired officers under trial for criticising the military.

Once the bill becomes law, the military would be required to release Robles, who has been detained on charges of "insubordination" since last week at a military barracks in Lima's neighbouring port of Callao.

The arrest of Robles, who linked an army "death-squad" to the recent bombing of a local television station, unleashed a political storm in Peru. Fujimori criticised the military for the arrest, calling it procedurally incorrect.

"Just as the Supreme Military Justice Council used its faculties (to arrest Robles), so I have used mine (to free him)," he said. That is precisely what gives balance to an authentically democratic system."

Defence Minister Tomas Castillo Meza told a Congressional hearing on Wednesday, that the military would agree to free Robles once the amnesty law came into affect, but he defended the way the arrest was conducted as legitimate.
"The capture took place without any abuse of human rights ... there was no ill-treatment nor use of toxic substances," he said.
Witnesses said the arrest was more like a kidnapping as eight people grabbed Robles, bundled him into a car and sprayed an aerosol can in his face to silence him.
Robles has frequently spoken out against Peru's military, which has maintained a delicate balance of power with Fujimori since his 1990 election.

After claiming an army "death squad" killed 10 students and a university teacher in 1992, Robles went into exile in Argentina to avoid trial but later returned to Peru when the government granted him an amnesty.
Human rights groups welcomed the general's imminent release. "This is a triumph for the people," said Francisco Soberon, director of Aprodeh, a local human rights group.
